nameStory: The Ipsilon Dart Moth gets its scientific name from the distinctive black markings on its forewings that look like the Greek letter upsilon (υ) or the letter "Y". The "dart" part of its name comes from its swift, darting flight pattern that's typical of many moths in this group.
description: The Ipsilon Dart Moth is a small, brown moth that's found worldwide and is incredibly common throughout New England. This unassuming little moth has brownish forewings marked with darker patterns, including the telltale Y-shaped marking that gives it its name. While the adult moths are fairly ordinary-looking, their caterpillars (called cutworms) are agricultural troublemakers that can chop down seedlings at soil level. The moths are part of a huge family called Noctuidae, which includes many of our most common nighttime flying moths.

idTips.label: Y-shaped wing marking
idTips.description: Look for distinctive black markings on the brown forewings that form a clear "Y" or upsilon shape - this is the moth's signature feature that's visible even on worn specimens

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: A small to medium-sized moth with a sturdy, compact body typical of cutworm moths - not delicate like many other night-flying species

idTips.label: Wing coloration
idTips.description: Forewings are typically brownish or grayish-brown with darker mottled patterns that help them blend into tree bark during the day

idTips.label: Flight behavior
idTips.description: Flies with quick, darting movements at night and is strongly attracted to artificial lights, often seen fluttering around porch lights and street lamps

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest during the day, holds wings roof-like over the body and blends remarkably well against brown surfaces like fence posts or tree bark

habitat: These adaptable moths can be found virtually anywhere in New England, from urban gardens to rural farmlands, forest edges to suburban yards. They're especially common around agricultural areas and gardens where their caterpillars feed on crops and vegetables. You'll encounter them in both disturbed habitats and more natural settings, as they're incredibly widespread and adaptable to different environments.

seasonality.spring: Adult moths begin appearing as temperatures warm, with migrants arriving from southern regions. This is peak mating season when you're most likely to see them at lights.
seasonality.summer: Adults continue to be active throughout the warm months, with multiple generations possible. Cutworm caterpillars are most noticeable now, cutting down garden plants at soil level.
seasonality.fall: Adults prepare for southward migration to escape harsh winter conditions. Late-season moths may still be active on warm evenings.
seasonality.winter: No activity in New England - these moths migrate south or die off, unable to survive our harsh winters.

funFact: These moths are incredible long-distance migrants that can travel hundreds of miles, riding wind currents from the southern United States all the way to Canada each spring, then making the return journey south in fall - making them the "snowbirds" of the moth world!
confusionNotes: The Ipsilon Dart Moth can be confused with many other brown nocturnal moths, but the distinctive Y-shaped marking on the forewings is your best bet for identification. Remember "Y for Ypsilon" - if you see that clear Y-pattern, you've got your moth!
contextualKnowledge: While the adult moths are harmless and even beneficial as pollinators, their caterpillars are serious agricultural pests known as "cutworms" because they literally cut young plants off at ground level. Gardeners often find their seedlings mysteriously chopped down overnight - that's usually the work of these moth larvae.
compareHints: Since this is the only Agrotis species commonly found in New England, compare it with other cutworm moths in the Noctuidae family. Most lack the distinctive Y-shaped marking that makes the Ipsilon Dart unique. Other cutworm moths tend to have more varied patterns of lines, spots, or kidney-shaped marks, but none have that clear upsilon symbol on their forewings.
